extracted.intended_audience: children and young readers who contribute letters, puzzles, drawings, and exchanges to Harper's Young People (late-19th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit submission criteria for contributors (children) writing letters, sending puzzles/exchanges, and participating in drawing exercises for Harper's Young People magazine. Covers what to include in letters, invited topics, puzzle contributions, and the drawing game 'Phizo.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Include full name (not merely initials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors are asked to give their full name rather than only initials when writing so the editor can remember them and follow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: "I like my boys to send more than their initials to me, so that I can remember them when they write again." Practical tip: supply a full name to facilitate future correspondence and recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell about your gardening successes and failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Little gardeners are explicitly invited to report on their gardening — both successes and failures — for the magazine's readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted invitation: "Now remember, little gardeners, that you are to have your turn, and tell us all about your successes and your failures." Use concrete details (what grew well, what failed) so other children can learn and be entertained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetable/fruit gardeners and young sellers: describe produce and business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetable and fruit gardeners should write about specific crops (lettuce, onions, radishes, strawberries) and children who earn money selling their produce are invited to explain how they manage those affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: "The vegetable and fruit gardeners may speak too. Let us hear about the lettuce, the onions, the radishes, and the strawberries. If there are any little business men or women who earn money of their own by selling the nice things they raise, they are invited to write and tell us how they manage their affairs." Guidance implies including quantities, prices, and methods of sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide vivid, specific local descriptions and anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters describing local life (e.g., floods, frontier life, foreign neighbors, pets, schoolrooms) should include concrete, interesting details that make the experience enjoyable and informative for other readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from page: flood description (depth measurements, animals lost), frontier activities (raising turkeys, trapping), neighborhood observations (Mexican neighbors, lava flows). Editor responses encourage further detail: "I shall expect another from you before a great while, telling all that is interesting about your Mexican neighbors." Aim for sensory/episodic detail that conveys the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send addresses when offering exchanges or requesting contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing exchanges (cards, coins, fossils, etc.) include a postal address so others can reply or send items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nettie Amelung signs with full street address: "NETTIE AMELUNG, 865 Lincoln Place, Brooklyn, N. Y." Practical guidance: include an address if you want to receive replies or to trade items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzles: submit puzzle entries with clear clues and expect published answers/acknowledgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers may submit puzzles (word squares, acrostics, diamonds, enigmas); the magazine publishes puzzles, provides solutions in later issues, and prints a list of correct solvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue prints multiple puzzle types with numbering, clues, and answers; it records correct solvers by (real or pen) names. Guidance implied: format puzzles clearly (label number and type), give unambiguous clues, and expect solution publication and acknowledgement (e.g., list of names who sent correct answers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phizo drawing exercise: required skill, method, and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Phizo is presented as a drawing game/exercise useful for practicing drawing and studying character; players should have some drawing skill and follow a specific play method (one person draws a profile, another describes it verbally, others draw from the description without seeing the original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive guidance from the article: "It is desirable that those engaging in this game should have some little skill in drawing." Procedure: one draws a profile of a head; a describer orally describes features (forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, chin, jaw, hair); others draw from that verbal description; then compare results. Purpose: "excellent practice and discipline in drawing and the study of character." The article supplies sample verbal descriptions to use as prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: When writing to the editor, respond to prompts and be willing to write follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor invites contributors to expand on subjects and sometimes asks for more detail in subsequent letters; contributors should be prepared to write follow-up letters when asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor prompts and replies appear throughout (e.g., "I shall expect another from you...", "we will be pleased to hear from you again"). Practical implication: if an editor requests more information, send a follow-up with the requested details or stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete personal anecdotes (pets, experiments, crafts) over vague statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors' letters that include concrete anecdotes about pets, experiments (making sugar), craftwork, or small adventures are treated as engaging and publishable rather than vague summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative passages: a boy describing making sugar (tapping trees, amount produced, money earned) and children writing about pets and their behaviors. Editorial reactions praise specificity and encourage similar contributions. Practical tip: include numbers, incident details, names of animals and actions to increase interest.
